title: Everyone does it, but how did you in particular train your AI to make art?
author: Claude_human_4271
selftext:
I mean everyone who has dabbled with 3D AI probably have their home-made skills, but how do you actually make **yours**? It would be very interesting to see how different specialized skills can affect the quality of different styles and objects.

I am just shooting wildly myself, and trying to see what sticks.  
I made some skills on design principles in general, composition and art theory. Then specialized game design principles such as common level design rules such as circular layouts, points of interest in big landscapes, etc. and then 3D design concepts such as how to make stylized fur from layered planes and that level of instructions.

I also provide it with a large library of sample 3D models and materials so that it can use them as references.

My output is... alright. But definitely not on the level of the online specialized 3D model AI's, so I'm wondering what I'm missing and I'm also a bit afraid that my Claude can start mixing up design rules between styles (such as realism vs impressionism).

So please, let me hear what you have done and how it has helped you and in which way you use these skills and instructions in your workflows.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
Train? Just make stylesheets like: this is what my character looks like.

comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
Shooting wildly and seeing what sticks is good exploratory time. I spent a lot of time on that for latest project before diving in, and keep iterating shit as I go too. IDK about skills files and so on, sorry. A level of "KISS" really does work imvvvho. In my experience, especially early in projects, rules etc can be restrictive in bad ways.  

I think, more than 'prompting for art theory/realism/impression' endlessly to ensure consistency you can just slowly build the right system for it, shaders, textures, whatever else. Reference art and talking it out can help a lot if you're struggling to find the vocab to describe a given thing. I'm going for painted/impressionistic look so for me it's lots of shaders and lighting, adding new geometry doesn't mean adding new art styles, because everything rendered gets painted the same way, if that makes sense? This can apply to any kinda art direction you want really - you can keep everything locked down and consistent using the game's "engine" rather than the AI itself and rebuild it ship of theseus style. Having that engine/system formalized into code also helps the AI itself see what the art direction is and stay consistent. It's a context prompt of its own.   
  
Hope that ramble helps :)

comments.author: jamurai
comments.body: Treat it like a game studio would: first do concept art, then turn that concept art into renders for 3d modeling (e.g. T Pose for characters,  multiple views, etc). For concept art keep refining and making edits. Direct not just the output but the style you are aiming for. After you get something you are happy with have the agent record the learnings + research + references into a reusable skill. Keep updating that skill when you find you have to make additional corrections. And experiment with different pipelines. For example: I use codex for concept art and final 2d renders. For characters and props I use tripo and rig in blender with auto rig pro. For buildings I found it better to have opus build the 3d and codex generate the textures and normal maps, and use tripo for building facades to make them more 3d in areas. For ground, similarly, codex generates the textures and the normal maps and opus implements into the game with the lighting

comments.author: Failosipher
comments.body:
Not really training, more of a pipeline where each tool does what it's good at. For my 3D stuff (mech RTS, Unity):

* concept art with an image model, then front/side/back views of the same design
* SIMPLIFY before going to 3D. Have the image model strip out all the bolts, greebles and grime but keep the silhouette. This was the big one for me. Detailed art gives you noisy geometry, simple art gives you clean meshes. Then once you have the simple model in Meshy and you've remeshed down to where you want to be, THEN re-texture with the high quality texture (the original gritty views). The detail goes into the texture, not the mesh.
* in Meshy that's multi-image to 3D with the simplified views → remesh → retexture with the detailed views
* Blender (headless) for low poly: remesh, decimate, rebake. Got an 8k tri rifle down to 1.4k and I really can't tell the difference lol

https://preview.redd.it/qmr73ukwmnwh1.jpeg?width=1400&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=e780c1cca2650d8b9b766413c385533f5f23909c

For keeping a style consistent: when I restyle a new concept to match an old one, I blur the new one first. The model keeps the shape but has to repaint the surface in the reference style. Without the blur it barely changes anything.

You can see how it all comes together in the devlogs: [https://failosipher.itch.io/engines-of-hate](https://failosipher.itch.io/engines-of-hate)
